subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
passage:
Incident note, primary health centre, Harigaon. Written by Zainab, community volunteer, 4 p.m.
At about 1 p.m. a forwarded voice message reached the village groups: "Child-lifters in a white van near the school. Stop them." By 1:30 around thirty people had surrounded Eshaan, a young surveyor measuring the road for the new drain, because his jeep was white. Someone grabbed his tape. The shouting grew as more people joined. Eshaan kept holding up his ID card; nobody looked at it.
I recognised his project letter from the panchayat notice board. I stood beside him, held the letter up high and asked the sarpanch's son to call the sarpanch and the police outpost. The police came at 2:10 and confirmed the survey. The message was two years old, from another district.
What I did next: I sat with Eshaan in the centre until he stopped shaking, and asked the sarpanch to send a correction to every village group this evening.

qa.q: Why did the crowd surround Eshaan?
qa.a: Because his jeep was white, matching the forwarded message.

qa.q: What was Zainab likely feeling while holding up the letter beside Eshaan?
qa.a: Zainab was probably frightened but determined, holding the facts while the crowd's anger was already rolling.

qa.q: Why was asking the sarpanch to send a correction important?
qa.a: The rumour was still sitting in every group; a clear correction from a trusted local voice could stop the next crowd.

qa.q: What was it like for Eshaan as the crowd grew?
qa.a: Eshaan was likely terrified and helpless, holding up an ID that nobody would even look at.

grounding: Shows an observer watching an old forwarded rumour turn a crowd against an innocent surveyor, with verified facts arriving only after the anger has started.

subtopic: Mob and crowd behaviour (stampede, riot, online pile-on)
passage:
I'm Tanvir, and I run a small baking page, so I've seen how fast the internet turns.
Last year my friend Zeenat posted a review of a café that she thought was fair. By morning, three thousand strangers were calling her a liar and worse; the café's fans had found her. Our friends' group was full of "Did you see?" and long public comments defending her, which only brought more people to the post.
I didn't comment. I messaged her: "I'm here. Don't read it. Want me to come over?" I went, with samosas. We sat on her floor, and I turned off her notifications. I reported the three accounts that posted her address and helped her block them. Mostly, we watched old cartoons.
She told me later that the public defences made her feel like a spectacle. The friend on her floor made her feel like a person.

qa.q: How many strangers were calling Zeenat a liar by morning?
qa.a: Three thousand strangers.

qa.q: How did the public defences make Zeenat feel?
qa.a: Zeenat felt exposed, "like a spectacle", even though her friends meant well.

qa.q: Which of Tanvir's steps mattered most?
qa.a: Messaging privately, being physically there, turning off notifications and reporting the accounts that shared her address.

qa.q: What would have changed if Tanvir had only posted a public defence?
qa.a: Zeenat would still be alone with her phone, and the post might have drawn even more strangers into the pile-on.

grounding: Shows a friend supporting a pile-on target with private messages, company, a break from the comments and reporting abuse, rather than public defence.

passage:
In the kindergarten in Osaka, Dalia marched up to Ms Tanaka before snack time. "Yuki took two crackers. And Ren splashed at the sink. And Hana didn't wash her hands." She stood very straight, waiting.
Ms Tanaka knelt. "Thank you, Dalia. Is anyone hurt or in danger?"
Dalia thought. "No."
"Then let's see if Yuki wants to share the extra cracker."
Dalia looked back at Yuki, who was holding both crackers and frowning at her. Dalia's smile wobbled.

qa.q: How many crackers did Yuki take?
qa.a: Yuki took two crackers.

qa.q: Why did Dalia stand very straight after telling?
qa.a: Dalia felt proud and was hoping for praise, waiting for Ms Tanaka to approve of her reporting.

qa.q: How did Ms Tanaka's question help Dalia?
qa.a: Asking "Is anyone hurt or in danger?" teaches Dalia the difference between telling to keep people safe and telling to get someone in trouble.

qa.q: How did Yuki seem to feel about Dalia's report?
qa.a: Yuki seemed annoyed, frowning at Dalia while holding the crackers.

grounding: Shows a young child announcing who broke small rules, mostly for adult approval, already sensing that news about others has social value.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was the BEST. Kabir, the new boy with the cool skateboard, sat with me at lunch!
I really wanted him to like me, so I told him a secret. Hansa still sleeps with a stuffed elephant called Motu, and she made me pinky-promise not to tell. Kabir laughed so much, and then he told Ishan, and they both laughed. Kabir said, "You know all the good stuff, Naveen." I felt like I was in the club.
After lunch Hansa was quiet and wouldn't look at me in art class. Maybe she's just tired.
Tomorrow Kabir says I can try his skateboard!!

qa.q: What is the name of Hansa's stuffed elephant?
qa.a: Motu.

qa.q: Why did Naveen tell Kabir the secret?
qa.a: Naveen felt excited and eager to be liked by the new boy, and sharing a secret felt like a way into his club.

qa.q: What could Naveen do tomorrow to make things right?
qa.a: Say sorry to Hansa, and tell Kabir and Ishan it was a secret that should not have been shared.

qa.q: What might Hansa be feeling in art class?
qa.a: Hansa is probably hurt and embarrassed, feeling betrayed that a pinky-promise was broken.

grounding: Shows a child sharing another's secret to feel close to a new friend, not seeing it as a betrayal of the one it concerns.

passage:
On the steps outside the Chennai coaching centre, Indu leaned in. "Guess who writes Arvind's name in the back of her rough book? Meena." Kavitha shrieked; Divya covered her mouth. For five whole minutes Indu was the centre of the circle, adding details: the little hearts, the way Meena went red in chemistry. It felt warm, being the one who knew things.
Then Meena herself walked past with her bag. The circle went silent, then burst into giggles. Meena looked at them, puzzled, and walked faster.
On the bus home, Indu scrolled through her phone. Kavitha had already sent "Meena + Arvind" to someone else. Indu stared at it. If they could pass on Meena's rough book this fast, what would they do with her own diary, the one Kavitha had flipped through last week?

qa.q: Whose name did Meena write in the back of her rough book?
qa.a: Arvind's name.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling on the bus home?
qa.a: Indu felt a nervous unease, worried the group might one day spread her own secrets just as fast.

qa.q: What could Indu do next time the group wants juicy news?
qa.a: Change the subject or keep other people's private things private, even if it means not being the centre of the circle.

qa.q: What was it like for Meena walking past the giggling circle?
qa.a: Meena felt puzzled and uncomfortable, sensing she was being laughed at without knowing why.

grounding: Shows a teenager gossiping about a peer's crush to bond with friends and gain status, enjoying it while fearing she could be next.

passage:
Baljeet,
You're the only one I can tell, since you're in Delhi now.
Since Monday, everyone at school is saying I copied in the prelims. That I had answers on my wrist. I didn't. I scored 92 because I spent the whole Diwali break on past papers. You KNOW I did; you were on video call with me half the time.
I don't know who started it. Could be anyone. Now when someone looks at me in the corridor my face goes hot and I want to sink into the floor. Yesterday Ritu and Sameer stopped talking when I sat down. I keep practising what I'd say if someone asked me straight out. Nobody does. They just whisper.
Uday
PS: After writing this I showed it to Appa. He read it twice, said this is not my fault, and emailed my class teacher tonight to ask for a meeting tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Uday score in the prelims?
qa.a: Uday scored 92.

qa.q: How does Uday feel walking through the corridor now?
qa.a: Uday feels hot shame and fear of every glance, wishing to sink into the floor.

qa.q: Why was showing the letter to Appa a good step?
qa.a: An adult could act the same day, reassuring Uday and asking the school to deal with a rumour Uday can't fight alone.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel reading this from Delhi?
qa.a: Baljeet may feel angry on Uday's behalf and helpless from far away, having seen the studying on video calls.

grounding: Shows a teenager who learns a false cheating rumour about them is spreading, feeling shame and fear of every glance without knowing who started it.

passage:
Monday: On the school bus, Nirmala leaned over. "Did you hear why Tara's parents came to school? Apparently..." Rashmi said, "I didn't hear, and I don't really want to. Did you finish the physics sheet?" Nirmala rolled her eyes. "Boring." Two girls behind them giggled.
Thursday: At lunch the story about Tara was everywhere, and Rashmi was left out of a whispered huddle. "She won't gossip anyway," someone said. Rashmi ate her lemon rice by herself.
Two weeks later, Saturday: Tara messaged Rashmi. "Can I talk to you? You're the only one who didn't pass that stuff around." They met on the library steps, and Tara talked for an hour. Walking home, Rashmi thought the lonely lunch had been worth it.

qa.q: What did Rashmi ask Nirmala instead of hearing the story?
qa.a: "Did you finish the physics sheet?"

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel eating lunch by herself on Thursday?
qa.a: Rashmi felt lonely and a bit left out, paying a small price for not joining the gossip.

qa.q: What made Rashmi's way of refusing work?
qa.a: She didn't lecture; she just said she didn't want to hear and changed the subject, so there was nothing to argue with.

qa.q: Why might Tara have chosen Rashmi to talk to?
qa.a: Tara trusted Rashmi as the one person who hadn't spread the story, so Rashmi felt safe 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager declining to hear a rumour and changing the subject, losing a little popularity but becoming someone safe to confide in.

passage:
I'm Zubin, and last month I nearly lost a friend over one sentence.
A few of us from drama club were in the canteen when Kunal said, "You know Shreya only got the lead because she's the director's cousin?" Everyone looked at me, because Shreya and I have been close since first year.
Part of me badly wanted to know if it was true. I even felt a flicker of "that explains it." Then a heavier feeling, like I was betraying her just by listening. I said, "I don't know that," and left my tea.
That evening I asked her straight: "People are saying you're related to the director. Is that true? I'd rather hear it from you."
She laughed, then went quiet. "He's my neighbour's son. I auditioned three times." Then she hugged me. "Thanks for asking me instead of them."

qa.q: What did Kunal claim about how Shreya got the lead?
qa.a: That she got it because she's the director's cousin.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Zubin have while listening to Kunal?
qa.a: Zubin felt curious, even a flicker of "that explains it", but also guilty, as if just listening betrayed Shreya.

qa.q: Why was checking with Shreya the wise choice?
qa.a: It got the facts from the person concerned, so Zubin didn't spread or believe a false story, and it kept their trust.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel about Zubin asking her directly?
qa.a: Shreya seemed hurt for a moment, then grateful, and hugged Zubin for asking her instead of the others 🤍

grounding: Shows a student told something unflattering about a friend, torn between curiosity and loyalty, choosing to check with the friend directly.

passage:
Asif,
You start at my college next month, so here's the guide I wish I'd had.
Professor Rao looks strict but is the fairest marker in the department. If you're stuck, go to her office hours; she'll spend an hour on one doubt.
Don't lend your lab notes to Vicky in third year. He borrowed mine twice and returned them once, with tea on page six. That's not me being mean. It's what happened, and I've said it to his face.
You'll hear plenty of other stuff in the hostel: who's dating whom, whose family has money, why someone dropped a year. Most of it is rubbish and none of it helps you. When the talk goes there, I go and make tea.
My rule: if it keeps you safe or saves you time, and I know it's true, I'll tell you. If it's just for laughs, I won't.
See you on the 3rd. Bring a bucket.
Wasim bhai

qa.q: Who is the fairest marker in the department?
qa.a: Professor Rao is the fairest marker in the department.

qa.q: How does Wasim seem to feel about the hostel gossip?
qa.a: Wasim seems fed up and uncomfortable with it, preferring to go and make tea rather than join in.

qa.q: What line does Wasim draw between useful talk and cruel gossip?
qa.a: Share something only if it is true and keeps Asif safe or saves time; skip anything that's just for laughs.

qa.q: How might Vicky feel if he read what Wasim wrote?
qa.a: Vicky might feel embarrassed or annoyed, but since it's accurate and already said to his face, it reads as a fair warning, not a cruel story.

grounding: Shows a young adult passing on accurate, useful information about people to a younger cousin while refusing gossip that only entertains.

passage:
By 10 a.m. on Monday, the pantry at the insurance office knew. "The Mumbai team's being merged with ours," said Priyanka, pouring tea, with the small smile of someone who'd heard first. "Three people are moving desks. I know who." Saurabh watched the circle tighten around her.
Vishal, at the next desk, wasn't in the pantry. He'd joined four months ago and wasn't in the unofficial lunch group. By noon he'd heard only half of it, "people moving". He refreshed his email every few minutes and asked Saurabh twice, "Did you hear anything about me?"
The official email from HR came at 5:30. Nobody on their floor was moving. Priyanka shrugged. "Well, it was close." Vishal breathed out as if he'd been holding it all day.
Saurabh decided that next time he heard something in the pantry, he'd ask where it came from before repeating it, and he'd make sure Vishal got invited to lunch.

qa.q: What time did the official email from HR arrive?
What did Saurabh feel watching Vishal refresh his email all day?
qa.a: Saurabh felt uneasy and sympathetic, seeing how the pantry talk left an outsider anxious while insiders felt important.

qa.q: What did Saurabh decide, and how could it help?
qa.a: To ask where news comes from before repeating it and to bring Vishal into lunch, which cuts false rumours and the gap between insiders and outsiders.

qa.q: What was the day like for Vishal?
qa.a: Vishal spent it anxious and on edge, hearing half a rumour and fearing it was about him until 5:30.

grounding: Shows a young professional watching news race through the pantry before any official word, empowering insiders and leaving outsiders anxious.
